content: The studies reviewed excluded those focusing on screening in blood banks and healthcare workers unless they also addressed subsequent linkage to care and treatment. Evaluations involving screening before vaccination were also excluded unless they considered antiviral therapy for individuals testing positive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). Additionally, studies on hepatitis B virus (HBV) screening prior to chemotherapy were excluded, as these are more relevant to high-income settings and a small subset of populations in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Studies examining co-infection with HIV or comparing diagnostic methods were also excluded. A PubMed search identified 32 studies, many of which overlapped with existing reviews. All studies were conducted in high-income countries (HICs), and no prior studies were found that described the cost or cost-effectiveness of HBV screening in LMICs. Ultimately, eight published studies and one unpublished study met the inclusion criteria and are discussed in detail. The existing literature on the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening and treatment has primarily been conducted in HICs, where the general population prevalence of HBV is low. The review also includes unpublished data from the PROLIFICA study, which is the only study conducted in a low-income country (LIC) setting. Two studies evaluated HBV screening in the general population, while seven studies focused on high-risk groups, most of which involved screening in migrant or refugee populations. Studies on antenatal care (ANC) screening were excluded because they did not consider antiviral therapy for mothers and only assessed the benefits of screening to guide vaccination strategies for reducing mother-to-child transmission. The studies used various screening methods for high-risk groups, including clinical settings, community outreach, and overseas screening. Many models were based on hypothetical cohorts. One U.S. study by Eckman et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of HBsAg testing in asymptomatic outpatients in primary care settings, using a hypothetical cohort of 35-year-old males with a 2% prevalence rate. Screening followed by treatment with one of four regimens was found to be cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $29,230 per QALY gained. A forthcoming study in The Gambia screened nearly 10,000 adults for HBsAg at the community level using active outreach, followed by clinical assessment and antiviral treatment for eligible individuals. This study reported an ICER of $705 per LY gained, $476 per QALY gained, or $575 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. Six studies examined the cost-effectiveness of screening and treatment in migrant or refugee populations in HICs, and one study in Italy evaluated screening all high-risk groups. For example, Wong et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of screening and treating immigrants for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in Canada. The screen and treat strategy had an ICER of $69,000 per QALY gained, which was considered cost-effective within the Canadian willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of $50,000–$120,000 per QALY. However, the model assumed high uptake and adherence rates, which may not be realistic. Another Canadian study by Rossi et al. found that a screen and treat strategy for newly arrived immigrants and refugees was the most cost-effective, with an ICER of $40,880 per QALY gained. However, this exceeded the Canadian WTP threshold when HBsAg prevalence was below 3%. The study used a societal perspective and assumed 70% screening acceptance, 60% linkage to care, and 75% treatment initiation among eligible individuals. Hutton et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening and vaccinating Asian Pacific Islander adults for HBV in the U.S., using a hypothetical cohort with a 10% HBsAg prevalence. The screen and treat strategy was the most cost-effective, with an ICER of $36,000 per QALY gained, even at a prevalence as low as 1%. A study by Rein et al. analyzed different screening methods for HBV among Asian migrants in the U.S., reporting costs per person screened ranging from $40 to $280, depending on the method. Integrating screening into clinical services was the least costly but reached fewer people, while community outreach was more expensive but had broader reach. Ruggeri et al. examined screening all high-risk groups in Italy, comparing the cost-effectiveness of screening followed by treatment for CHB using various antiviral drugs. Screening and treatment had an ICER of €17,000 per QALY gained, compared to the status quo of no screening. Studies on ANC screening for HBsAg primarily focused on reducing mother-to-child transmission and benefits to the child, without considering onward care or treatment for the mother. These studies are not included in detail, as they are less relevant to guiding current recommendations for HBV screening and treatment in ANC settings in LMICs. Key drivers of cost-effectiveness identified in the reviewed studies include HBsAg prevalence, costs of screening and treatment, adherence to treatment, and linkage to care. While HBsAg prevalence had a relatively small influence on cost-effectiveness across wide ranges, adherence to treatment and linkage to care were significant factors. The age of the screened cohort also influenced cost-effectiveness, with younger populations generally yielding more favorable ICERs. However, ethical considerations around age cut-offs should be taken into account. The effectiveness of antiviral therapy was another important factor, with newer drugs like tenofovir and entecavir showing high efficacy. However, assumptions about antiviral efficacy in LMICs need further validation, as most efficacy data originate from HICs. In conclusion, while the reviewed studies provide valuable insights, their applicability to LMICs is limited due to differences in healthcare structures, costs, and disease prevalence. Cost-effectiveness analyses specific to LMIC settings are needed to guide HBV screening and treatment strategies effectively.
